paragraphs.text: Every autumn, the forests of the temperate world stage a display that has been admired for as long as people have written about trees, and explained properly for only a few decades. Green leaves turn yellow, orange and red over a few weeks, then fall. The change is so regular that it is easy to assume it is simply a matter of leaves dying, but the process is more organised than that, and some of the colours are produced deliberately, at a cost to the tree, in the last days of the leaf’s life. Understanding it requires looking at each colour separately, because they do not all arise in the same way.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The green of a summer leaf comes from chlorophyll, the pigment that captures light for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll is constantly being broken down and replaced while the leaf is active, and it is expensive to make, because each molecule contains nitrogen, one of the nutrients trees find hardest to obtain. As days shorten and temperatures fall, the tree stops replacing it and begins to dismantle it in an orderly way, recovering the nitrogen and moving it into the branches and roots, where it will be stored over winter and used to build new leaves in spring. The whole operation takes several weeks, and it follows a sequence that is remarkably similar across different species.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The yellows and oranges were in the leaf all along. They come from pigments called carotenoids, which help chlorophyll gather light and protect the leaf from damage caused by strong sunlight. In summer they are hidden by the far greater quantity of green; as the chlorophyll is removed, they become visible. Because carotenoids are broken down more slowly, the yellow phase can last for a week or more, and species whose leaves turn only yellow, such as birch and many poplars, are simply revealing what the green had concealed. The same pigments give carrots and many flowers their colour.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Red is a different matter. The red and purple pigments, called anthocyanins, are largely absent from summer leaves and are manufactured in autumn, at exactly the time the tree is trying to recover resources from the leaf. Why a tree should spend energy making a new pigment in a leaf it is about to discard has been a puzzle for botanists. The quantity produced varies with the weather: bright, dry days followed by cool nights produce the most intense reds, which is why some regions and some years are famous for their colour and others are not.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The most widely supported explanation is that anthocyanins act as a kind of sunscreen. While the leaf is dismantling its chlorophyll, its capacity to use light falls, and strong sunlight on cold days can damage the cells before the recovery of nutrients is complete. A layer of red pigment absorbs some of that light and allows the process to continue for longer. Experiments that shaded some leaves and not others found that red leaves under full sun recovered more nitrogen than yellow leaves of similar species, which supports the idea, though the size of the benefit varies considerably.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: A second explanation, still debated, concerns insects. Aphids that lay their eggs on trees in autumn prefer yellow leaves, and it has been suggested that a bright red display signals to them that the tree is healthy and well defended, discouraging them from choosing it. Some comparisons across species have found that trees with the reddest autumn leaves tend to host fewer aphid species, but others have found no such pattern, and the two explanations are not mutually exclusive: a pigment can protect the leaf and send a signal at the same time. Researchers who favour the signalling idea note that it would help explain why red is so much more common in some regions than in others.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Once nutrients have been withdrawn, the leaf is cut off. A layer of cells forms at the base of the leaf stalk, weakening it until wind or the weight of the leaf itself breaks the connection, and the scar is sealed to keep out disease. The browns of a leaf on the ground come from substances that remain after the other pigments have broken down. Some trees, notably young oaks and beeches, keep their dead leaves attached through much of the winter, a habit that may protect buds from grazing animals, though this too has not been proved. The timing of this separation is controlled by hormones that respond to the length of the day.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Climate change is already affecting the display. In many regions leaves are changing colour and falling later than they did several decades ago, while very warm or dry autumns can cut the colour short, with leaves browning and dropping before the reds have developed. The consequences go beyond the scenery. A longer growing season allows trees to absorb more carbon in some places, but trees that keep their leaves late are exposed to early frosts that can kill the leaf before its nitrogen has been recovered, leaving the tree with less to invest the following spring. Predicting how the display will change is therefore a question about nutrients as much as about scenery.
paragraphs.label: H

paragraphs.text: For most of urban history, a fire was everyone’s problem and nobody’s responsibility. Towns built largely of wood, heated by open flames and lit by candles burned regularly, sometimes almost completely, and the response depended on whoever happened to be nearby. Householders were often required by law to keep buckets and ladders, and bells summoned neighbours to form lines passing water from the nearest well or river. Such efforts could save a single house if the fire was caught early; once flames spread across a street, there was little anyone could do except pull down buildings in their path to create a gap. Fire was, for most town dwellers, the most serious danger they faced after disease.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The first organised services were often commercial rather than public. In several European cities in the eighteenth century, insurance companies established their own teams of firefighters, equipped with hand-operated pumps and paid to protect the buildings the companies had insured. Insured properties displayed a metal plate on the front wall so that the teams could identify them. The popular story that these brigades would watch an uninsured house burn is probably exaggerated, since a fire left alone would soon threaten insured buildings nearby, but the arrangement did mean that protection followed payment rather than need. Some companies also cooperated, sending teams to fires at buildings insured by rivals in the expectation of the same help in return.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Technical improvements gradually increased what a team could achieve. Hand pumps grew larger and could throw water higher, leather hoses allowed water to be directed through doorways and windows rather than simply thrown, and piped water supplies under city streets, installed mainly for drinking and sanitation, gave firefighters a reliable source close to most buildings. Steam-powered pumps, introduced in the mid-nineteenth century, could deliver far more water than any team of men working levers, although they were at first opposed by some firefighters who feared for their jobs. Horses soon replaced the men who had pulled the engines through the streets.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The shift to public services came through a combination of disaster and reform. Large urban fires in the nineteenth century, which destroyed thousands of buildings regardless of who had insured them, persuaded city authorities that fire protection was a public good that could not be left to private arrangements. One after another, cities created municipal brigades paid from local taxes, took over the equipment and staff of the insurance teams, and made protection available to every building. By the end of the century, a public fire service had become one of the standard features of a modern city. The transition was not always smooth, since some insurance teams resisted the loss of their role.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Professionalisation followed. Early municipal brigades often included volunteers and part-time men with other jobs, and discipline could be poor. Reformers introduced full-time crews living at the station, regular drills, ranks borrowed from the navy and the army, and systematic training in how fire behaves in buildings. The goal was speed: a crew that could leave the station within a minute of an alarm would reach most fires before they had spread beyond a single room. Telegraph alarm boxes placed on street corners, and later telephones, shortened the time between discovery and response still further. Some brigades began keeping detailed records of every call, which later proved valuable to historians of urban life.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Perhaps the most important change, however, took place not in the fire service but in the buildings. Regulations requiring brick or stone walls between neighbouring houses, limits on wooden construction in city centres, and later rules on fire escapes, fire doors and materials that do not burn easily reduced the number of fires that could spread at all. Historians of the subject increasingly argue that building codes saved more lives and property than improvements in firefighting, even though they receive far less attention in popular accounts, which tend to focus on dramatic rescues. Insurers, who had most to gain, were among the strongest supporters of such rules.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The work of a modern fire service reflects this history. In many countries firefighters now spend more of their time on prevention than on fires: inspecting buildings, fitting smoke alarms in homes, and teaching schoolchildren what to do in an emergency. They also respond to road accidents, floods and chemical spills, which in some areas outnumber fires by a large margin. The number of domestic fires has fallen substantially in many places over recent decades, a decline usually credited to smoke alarms, safer electrical appliances and a sharp reduction in smoking indoors.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The story of the fire brigade is often told as one of heroism, and the bravery involved is real. But it is also a story about how a society decides that a risk is shared. The move from buckets carried by neighbours, through protection bought by those who could afford it, to a service available to all and funded by all, reflects a change in how cities understood their obligations to the people living in them. The same question, of which risks should be pooled and which left to individuals, continues to be argued about in other areas of public policy. Few public services show that argument as clearly as the one that answers the alarm.
paragraphs.label: H

texts.title: Do standardised tests measure what matters?

paragraphs.text: Few features of modern education provoke as much argument as the standardised test. Examinations taken by every pupil of a given age, marked against the same criteria and reported as numbers, are used to decide university places, to compare schools and, in some systems, to judge teachers. Critics say they narrow what is taught and reward preparation rather than understanding; defenders say they are the fairest instrument available for comparing pupils who attend very different schools. Both sides often write as though the question had a single answer, when the evidence suggests that it depends a great deal on what the test is used for. Assessing it fairly means considering each purpose in turn.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Lena Hoffmann, who studies assessment, argues that the most important distinction is between a test’s purpose and its consequences. A well-designed test can give a reasonably accurate picture of what pupils know in a subject at a particular moment, she says, and that information is valuable to teachers and families. The difficulty arises when heavy consequences are attached to the results, because the more a number matters, the more effort goes into raising the number rather than the learning it was meant to reflect. In her view, most of the damage attributed to testing is really caused by the uses to which results are put. She compares a test to a thermometer: useful for reading the temperature, but misleading if people start warming the instrument instead of the room.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The narrowing of the curriculum is the complaint heard most often from teachers. Samuel Adeyemi, a former head teacher who now researches school policy, found that in schools where test results determined funding or inspection grades, time spent on subjects that were not tested, such as art, music and history, fell substantially over several years. Within tested subjects, lessons shifted towards the kinds of questions that appeared in the examination. He does not claim that this preparation is useless, since pupils did improve on the skills being tested, but argues that the gains were narrower than the headline figures implied.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Defenders respond that the alternatives are not obviously better. Ruth Castellano, an economist who has studied university admissions, points out that when tests are removed, selection relies more heavily on teachers’ assessments, personal statements and interviews, all of which are influenced by the resources of a pupil’s family and school. In her analysis of institutions that dropped test requirements, the share of students from poorer backgrounds did not rise and in some cases fell. A test, she argues, is at least the same test for everyone, whatever its limitations. She acknowledges, however, that access to test preparation is itself unequal, since families who can pay for tutoring gain an advantage.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The question of what tests leave out is harder to settle. Skills such as working with others, persisting with a difficult task or solving an unfamiliar problem are widely believed to matter for later life, and they are poorly captured by timed written papers. Kenji Morita, who designs assessments, has worked on tasks that attempt to measure such qualities, including extended projects and collaborative problems. He reports that these can be done, but that they are expensive to mark consistently, take far longer than a conventional paper, and are harder to protect against coaching once their format becomes known. Some universities have experimented with such tasks alongside conventional tests rather than instead of them.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Reliability is a further concern that receives less public attention than it deserves. Every test measures with some error, and a pupil’s score on a given day may differ from the score they would obtain on another day by more than the gap between two grade boundaries. Hoffmann notes that when single results are used to make decisions about individuals, such as whether a pupil is admitted to a particular school, this uncertainty is rarely communicated to the families concerned, who tend to treat the number as far more precise than it is. A result reported with its margin of error looks less authoritative, which may be one reason it is so rarely done.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Several systems have tried to preserve the advantages of testing while limiting its side effects. Some test only a sample of pupils in order to monitor national standards, which removes the incentive for any individual school to prepare intensively. Others combine examination results with coursework or teacher assessment, or report results in broad bands rather than precise scores. Adeyemi considers sample testing the most promising of these approaches for judging the system as a whole, although it provides no information about individual pupils, which is precisely what families and universities want. Each of these compromises gives up something in exchange for what it gains.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The argument about standardised testing is therefore less about the tests themselves than about the weight placed on them. A test used to inform teachers, taken seriously but without high stakes, is hard to object to; a test on which a school’s survival or a pupil’s future entirely depends will distort the behaviour of everyone around it. The practical question for any education system is not whether to test but how much to rely on the results, and how honestly to report what a single number can and cannot tell. Those are questions of judgement, not of measurement.
paragraphs.label: H
